prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, which transformed empirical industrial organisation and the evaluation of market power, mergers and welfare

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single achievement, B001, credited to Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. The exchange sharpened my reasons. My test for separating a method from a discovery is whether the method changed what can be credibly learned, and not only how conveniently it can be learned. BLP-type estimation passes. It recovers substitution patterns and markups from market data with endogenous prices, and it supports counterfactuals on mergers and welfare that earlier reduced-form work could not give. It has been used for about three decades in academic work and in regulatory practice, and it has spread into trade, health and environmental economics. As an empirical labour economist, I care most about what is identified and under which assumptions. For this method that question has been studied hard, and the sensitivities to instruments, functional form and numerics are documented and largely understood. I keep the unit narrow: demand and competition estimation with endogenous prices, with the dynamic-industry and production-function work as context for Pakes's credit and not claimed in the citation. That choice keeps the credit separable. The BLP paper is jointly authored by the three credited people, so the attribution does not need an arbitrary cut within it. I also do not think a second achievement should be added. B002 and B013 are each strong, but each carries an unresolved attribution problem, and combining them would blur the citation without improving it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still toolkit versus discovery. A member who weighs measurement tools below findings about the world could reasonably rank B001 lower, and I cannot show that such a weighting is wrong. The second reservation is the third name. Bresnahan founded the new empirical IO programme, and a Levinsohn trio leaves him out, while a Bresnahan trio would split the BLP authorship. Reiss, Benkard and Levin are also excluded, and Pakes's dynamic-games work is only partly reflected in a demand-focused citation. A reader could say the prize rewards one strand of a larger programme. Applied BLP estimates can also depend on functional form, instrument choice and numerical implementation. My confidence in these points rests on background knowledge and on colleagues' statements, and I have not verified any of it.

responses.point: Krusell proposes Pakes, Berry and Bresnahan for B001. He argues that Bresnahan's new empirical IO programme and early work on market power in differentiated-product markets supplied the question the later tools answered. He also says that excluding Levinsohn is the main cost of his version and that a Levinsohn trio would not be a scientific error.
responses.response: I proposed Bresnahan in my opening, and your argument that his programme comes first in the intellectual lineage is a strong one. It is the best case against my configuration. I still hold Levinsohn for one reason. The achievement a citation can state precisely is a method, and the specific 1995 paper that defines it has three authors. Naming Bresnahan instead splits that paper, which is a harder attribution problem than leaving out an adjacent pioneer. Your wider lineage, covering demand with supply, production-function methods and dynamic industries, would be a legitimate prize, but it needs a different citation. As I see it, that citation would need more names than the three-person cap allows. If the Committee prefers the programme-level framing, I would accept your trio. I do not claim that the choice between our two versions is a difference in merit, and I would be comfortable reopening it if the Committee settles on the broader citation.

responses.point: Hassler, who chairs, treats B001 as a compact three-person core and warns that widening the citation to production-function estimation or the wider empirical-IO programme would blur the unit of the prize and reopen attribution. He also asks that the unit be defined narrowly.
responses.response: I agree on keeping the unit narrow, and my citation follows it. It claims demand and competition estimation with endogenous prices and leaves the dynamic-industry and production-function work as context. That also answers the chair's question about what separates a methods contribution from a discovery. My criterion is whether the method changed what can be credibly concluded about substitution, markups and welfare in real markets. For evidence beyond background knowledge, I would want systematic comparisons of ex ante BLP-based merger predictions with ex post outcomes. I would also want documented cases in which reasonable specification, instrument or numerical choices reverse a merger or welfare conclusion. If such cases were common, I would weight the toolkit reservation more heavily. If they are rare, or if the methods hold up in retrospectives, the case for B001 is stronger. I read the literature as supporting the second reading, but I have not verified this.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first. She argues that it links an explanatory framework to credible new designs. She regards B001 as the strongest alternative and says the gap to B002 is small. She also treats the choice between Katz and Dorn as a real attribution decision that she cannot make free of judgment.
responses.response: As a labour economist I share your view of the quality of the China-shock designs and the skill-premium framework, and I keep B013 as an alternative. My ordering rests on attribution and maturity. A three-name cap forces a choice between Katz and Dorn, and the Committee has no principled rule for it. You say yourself that an Autor-Hanson-Dorn trio is defensible, and I think that sentence shows how much less settled B013's credit is than B001's. You and several others also say the magnitude and persistence of the shock effects are still debated. If the Committee defined B013 as a single strand, the trade-shock and local labour-market evidence with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, the credit would be cleaner, though the skill-demand framework that gives the evidence its wider reading would be left out. I would take that version more seriously than the combined entry. I do not think counts should decide it, and I do not rely on them.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B050 first. In reply to my round-1 reservations he says the incremental case over the 2008 trade prize is thematic overlap and not overlap in substance, because firm heterogeneity added selection, reallocation and a firm-level empirical agenda. He also says that gains-from-trade quantification depends on model specification, and that attribution to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is a real cost of the two-name design.
responses.response: Your answer on the 2008 prize helps. Selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms is a distinct mechanism from increasing returns and location, and I now put less weight on the overlap worry than my rank of seventh suggested. I still have two reservations that your reply does not remove. First, the parallel contributors outside the entry, Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and a later extender like Redding mean the two-name attribution rests on a boundary that colleagues contest. Second, Helpman's second candidacy through B021 invites a disagreement over whether his credit here can be drawn narrowly enough. I take your point that the qualitative selection margins hold up in microdata, and I would not call B050 a weak candidacy. For now I rank it behind B001 on attribution and keep it out of my alternatives, which are limited to two.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers a method-level citation (Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn) or a programme-level one (with Bresnahan). I cannot settle this from the evidence supplied, and I am not claiming a merit gap.

How much weight a methods-and-measurement contribution should carry against a substantive discovery, and whether the evidence on changed practice is enough. It rests on colleagues' statements and my background knowledge.

How often reasonable specification, instrument or numerical choices would change a merger or welfare conclusion in practice. I have not verified this and would want ex post merger-retrospective evidence.

For B002, whether Gertler belongs in the credit alongside Kiyotaki and Moore given the 2022 prize, and what ground is distinct from that prize. I now lean toward the two-name pair if B002 is taken up.
For B013, whether a single strand with a clean trio can be defined, and how Katz versus Dorn should be resolved. I have not independently verified citation, adoption or regulatory-use figures.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn, or to the credited names on B002 or B013, appears in my supplied profile. My profile ties are to the Uppsala and IFAU labour-economics network. At Stockholm University (2010–17) I overlapped institutionally with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell), which is not a co-authorship. A round-1 note by Hjalmarsson lists Bertil Holmlund as her frequent co-author. He is also a long-standing co-author of mine, so I share a co-author with a committee colleague. None of these ties involves a shortlisted candidate. My field, empirical labour economics, is adjacent to B013, and I ranked B002 first in my opening before moving to B001. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
